content: Lipases are water-soluble enzymes that facilitate the hydrolysis of ester bonds in lipid substrates that are insoluble in water. These enzymes belong to a subclass of esterases and are found ubiquitously across living organisms. Interestingly, genes encoding lipases are also present in certain viruses. Most lipases act on specific positions of the glycerol backbone of lipid substrates, such as positions A1, A2, or A3. For example, human pancreatic lipase (HPL), the primary enzyme responsible for fat digestion in the human digestive system, converts triglycerides from dietary oils into monoglycerides and free fatty acids. Beyond this, lipases exhibit a wide range of activities in nature, particularly when considering phospholipases and sphingomyelinases. Structurally, lipases are diverse, with various genetically distinct forms found in nature. Despite this diversity, most lipases share a common alpha/beta hydrolase fold and utilize a chymotrypsin-like hydrolysis mechanism. This mechanism typically involves a serine nucleophile, an acidic residue (commonly aspartic acid), and a histidine residue. Lipases function in different locations within the body. Some operate within the intracellular environment, such as lysosomal lipase, which is confined to the lysosome organelle. Others, like pancreatic lipases, act extracellularly and play critical roles in lipid metabolism, absorption, and transport throughout the body. Given that biological membranes are primarily composed of phospholipids, lipases are integral to cell biology. They are also involved in a variety of biological processes, ranging from the routine metabolism of dietary triglycerides to cell signaling and inflammation. In humans, the primary lipases in the digestive system are human pancreatic lipase (HPL) and pancreatic lipase-related protein 2 (PLRP2), both secreted by the pancreas. Additionally, humans possess other related enzymes, such as hepatic lipase (HL), endothelial lipase, and lipoprotein lipase. Not all of these enzymes function in the gastrointestinal tract. Other lipases include LIPH, LIPI, LIPJ, LIPK, LIPM, and LIPN. There is also a wide variety of phospholipases, though these are not always classified alongside other lipases. Lipases derived from fungi and bacteria have historically played significant roles in human practices, such as yogurt and cheese fermentation. In modern applications, lipases are being utilized as cost-effective and versatile catalysts for lipid degradation. For instance, recombinant lipase enzymes have been developed for use in industries such as baking, laundry detergents, and even as biocatalysts in alternative energy strategies, such as converting vegetable oil into biofuels.
